report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is *plausible but not established with high certainty*. Small randomized trials suggest that acupuncture designed specifically for depression can reduce symptoms during pregnancy, but the evidence base is limited and does not show that acupuncture is superior to all credible alternatives.

The largest identified randomized trial enrolled 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder and compared depression-specific acupuncture with nonspecific acupuncture and massage. It reported that depression-specific acupuncture produced greater symptom improvement than the combined controls, so it is meaningful supportive evidence. An earlier pilot trial was much smaller (61 women), explicitly limiting generalizability.  
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15546651/

Important caveats: acupuncture trials are difficult to blind fully, “nonspecific” acupuncture or massage may not be inert, and there appear to be few large, independently replicated trials. A later study found in search results was a *trial protocol*, rather than outcome evidence, indicating that research has still been developing.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26887958/

Clinical guidelines for perinatal mental health emphasize detection and evidence-based management; acupuncture is not presented as a standard first-line treatment for antenatal depression in the NICE recommendations. Do not use it as a replacement for assessment, psychotherapy, medication when indicated, or urgent care for suicidal thoughts. It could be considered an adjunct if the obstetric and mental-health clinicians agree and the practitioner is qualified.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/recommendations
